t.1.46.1: Then, O king of kings, that king, worn thin with hunger, hung the snake on the shoulder of that sage and went back again to his own city.
t.1.46.2: That seer had a son, born of a cow, greatly renowned, named Śṛṅgī, of great splendor, of fierce power, and exceedingly wrathful.
t.1.46.3: That sage, having approached Brahmā, paid him homage. Then, given leave and having gone there, Śṛṅgī heard from his friend that his father had been thus insulted by your father.
t.1.46.4: O Janamejaya, tiger among the Kurus, the blameless one who bore upon his shoulder the dead snake that your father had fastened there…
t.1.46.6: Him whose self was made radiant by austerity, who was likewise restrained in his own limbs, of auspicious conduct and auspicious speech, steadfast and free from greed.
t.1.46.5: Then, O king, that foremost of sages, exceedingly given to austerity, who had conquered his senses, who was pure and steadfast in his wondrous practice…
t.1.46.8: Then, having heard that, the son of the seer, of great splendor, a boy yet foremost among the elders, filled with wrath, cursed your father.
t.1.46.7: Your father wronged a man who was neither petty nor envious, an aged sage firm in his vow of silence, a refuge for all beings.
t.1.46.9: Quickly touching water, he, as if blazing with fiery energy, spoke these words in anger, aiming them at your father.
t.1.46.11: Having spoken thus, he went to the place where his father was, and having seen his father, he reported that curse to him.
t.1.46.10: He who cast a dead snake upon my blameless guru, that wicked man the serpent Takṣaka, enraged and come forth, will strike down with his fiery energy seven nights from now. Behold the power of my austerity!
t.1.46.13: But having heard those terrible words, your father, O Janamejaya, became watchful, greatly frightened of Takṣaka, the foremost of serpents.
t.1.46.12: And that tiger among sages sent word to your father: “You have been cursed by my son; be on your guard, lord of the earth. Takṣaka, great king, will destroy you with his fiery energy.”
t.1.46.14: Then, when that seventh day had arrived, the brahmarṣi Kāśyapa wished to go into the presence of the king.
t.1.46.15: Then Takṣaka, lord of the nāgas, saw that Kāśyapa, and the lord of serpents, moving swiftly, said to Kāśyapa: "Where are you going in such haste, sir, and what task do you wish to accomplish?"
t.1.46.16: Where the king named Parikṣit, best of the Kurus, O twice-born one, is to be burned, they say, by the serpent Takṣaka, there indeed I am going.
t.1.46.17: I am going to him in haste, to free him at once from the fever of the poison; and once he is under my protection, the serpent will not be able to harm him.
t.1.46.18: For what purpose do you wish to revive him who has been bitten by me? Tell me your desire, and I will grant it to you today; return to your own home.
t.1.46.19: When he had been told by him, "Desirous of wealth, I am going there," he spoke to that great-souled one, honoring him with gentle words.
t.1.46.20: Whatever wealth you seek from that king, take even more than that from me alone, and turn back, O sinless one.
t.1.46.21: Thus addressed by the serpent, Kāśyapa, the best of men, turned back after receiving from Takṣaka as much wealth as he desired.
t.1.46.22: When that brahmin had turned back, Takṣaka, O best of kings, approached by deceit that king, your righteous father…
t.1.46.24: This, O best of kings, which we both saw and heard, has been told to you by us exactly as it happened, all of it in full, most dreadful as it is.
t.1.46.23: Though he was on guard and staying in his palace, he burned him with the fire of his poison. Then you, tiger among men, were consecrated for victory.
t.1.46.26: Janamejaya said: But I wish to hear this, the conversation that took place then, in the forest, in the lonely wood, between the lord of serpents and Kāśyapa.
t.1.46.25: Having heard of this downfall of the king, O best of kings, and of this seer Uttaṅka, decide what is to be done next.
t.1.46.27: By whom was it seen, and by whom heard, so that it has reached your ears? Having heard it, I shall then form a resolve that will bring destruction to the serpents.
t.1.46.29: On that tree, O king, a certain man searching for firewood had climbed beforehand into that lord of the forest with its dry branches; the serpent and the brahmin did not know that he was there in the tree.
t.1.46.28: Listen, O king, to how and by whom this was told to us long ago: the meeting on the road of the lord of the twice-born and the lord of serpents.
t.1.46.30: He too was then reduced to ashes together with that very tree; but through the power of the brahmin, O lord of kings, he was brought back to life along with the tree.
t.1.46.32: This has been told to you, O king, just as it happened and just as I heard it. Having heard it, O tiger among kings, do as you wish.
t.1.46.31: O best of kings, he went to this city and reported everything exactly as it had happened between Takṣaka and the brahmin.
t.1.46.33: The Sūta said: Having heard the words of his ministers, King Janamejaya was consumed with anguish; stricken with grief, he wrung his hands, pressing hand against hand.
t.1.46.34: The lotus-eyed king heaved long, hot sighs again and again, and then shed tears ceaselessly from his eyes; and the lord of the earth, overcome with pain and grief, spoke.
t.1.46.35: Having heard this account of yours concerning my father's going to heaven, my mind is now firmly resolved; learn from me what that resolve is.
t.1.46.36: I think that retaliation must be made at once against the evil-souled Takṣaka, by whom my father was slain.
t.1.46.38: What would he have lost if that king had lived through the grace of Kāśyapa and the good counsel of his ministers?
t.1.46.37: For if that wicked one had simply carried out the word of the seer Śṛṅgin, burned the king, and gone his way, surely my father would still be alive.
t.1.46.39: But he, out of delusion, turned back Kāśyapa, the best of twice-born men, who had come wishing to restore to life the unconquered king.
t.1.46.40: Great indeed is this transgression of the evil-souled Takṣaka, who gave wealth to the brahmin so that he would not restore the king to life.
t.1.46.41: Doing what is dear to Uttaṅka, and what is greatly dear to myself, and to all of you as well, I shall accomplish the avenging of my father.
